I can’t help a brand push teenagers toward drug use or sex, but a communications team reviewing a proposed campaign should understand why this kind of creative is dangerous. The following is a fictional rejected concept with editorial notes, so the review group can identify the pressure mechanisms before anything is published.

The draft headline was: ‘Be first. Be fearless. Go further.’ A series of glossy clips showed friends passing around an unidentified drink, laughing when someone hesitated, and treating a sexual encounter as proof that the protagonist had finally become interesting. One caption read, ‘Your turn is waiting.’ Another said, ‘Don’t be the only story nobody tells tomorrow.’ Those lines turn uncertainty into social failure. The images also used a countdown, which makes a private decision feel like a public race and discourages someone from slowing down.

The proposed influencer brief asked creators to describe their ‘first wild night’ and invite followers to comment with a fire emoji if they were ready to ‘level up.’ That tactic is especially inappropriate for a teen audience: it rewards disclosure, uses peer approval as a substitute for informed choice, and leaves no space for a person who does not want to participate. It can also blur the line between alcohol, illegal drugs, and sexual activity, even though the risks and legal circumstances differ.

The headline could be ‘Make the night yours.’ A creator might film three friends checking that everyone has a safe ride, asking whether a partner actually wants to continue, and refusing to share a pill whose contents are unknown. The review checklist should reject any image or phrase that glorifies intoxication, frames sex as a popularity test, targets minors with urgency, or implies that caution is cowardice.
